text:
I would like to know if there were 450 citizens killed. I never found out anything. I did find that they had buried 450 civilians at the base of the mountain that they found a mass grave later on after the war was over. The mountain name is Nui Ba Din. This was at the end of my service. I was medivac out a couple days later. 

When I got back to duty at Ton Son Nuht and I went to a medic that was right to my workstation and told him I felt sick and he said no wonder, you have yellow jaundice. I was at Camp Zama in Japan in Sugami Uro.
researchNotes: Two significant items. (1) He produced "Camp Zama" unprompted — at the table he was told only that research had a high-confidence hospital name, not what it was — independently confirming the Camp Zama / Sagami-Ōno identification ("Sugami Uro" is read as Sagami-Ōno; see research/places/japan-hospital-1965.md). (2) The sequencing: the accusation came at the end of his service; back at Tân Sơn Nhứt a medic diagnosed yellow jaundice ("no wonder"), and he was medevaced a couple of days later — placing the Núi Bà Đen incident days before his ~early-September 1965 departure. The mass-grave account (450 civilians buried at the base of the mountain, found after the war) is a researchable claim; no source has been located yet (research/events/450-civilians-nui-ba-den.md).
